stem: A team's fan chatbot relies on one carefully tuned system prompt for its whole guardrail strategy. Before a playoff marketing push, the CISO asks what should be added so that a single clever message can't defeat every protection at once. What is the best answer?

options.text: A longer system prompt that spells out every forbidden topic in more detail.
options.explanation: Making the prompt longer still leaves a single advisory layer. Prompts guide behavior, but they don't enforce it.

options.text: A copy of the system prompt repeated at the end of every user turn.
options.explanation: Repeating the same instructions adds emphasis, not an independent layer. An attack that beats the prompt once can beat it twice.

options.text: Input screening, output checks and tool limits enforced outside the model.
options.explanation: Correct. Independent layers fail in different ways, so an attack has to beat all of them, and the strongest limits are enforced in code and infrastructure.

options.text: A friendlier refusal message so that users are less inclined to argue.
options.explanation: A better refusal script improves the experience but adds no protection against a determined attacker.

stem: A ticketing support assistant screens every message with a moderation classifier. Under Sunday game-day load the classifier sometimes times out, and an engineer proposes letting messages through unscreened on timeout so fans don't wait. What should the design do?

options.text: Fail closed: hold or reject the message when screening errors, and alert on timeouts.
options.explanation: Correct. Secure-by-design guardrails fail closed. A screen that silently switches off under load is exactly when attackers would strike, and alerts let the team fix capacity.

options.text: Fail open on timeouts, but log each unscreened message so someone can review it next week.
options.explanation: Reviewing a week later is detection, not prevention. Harmful requests would already have been answered.

options.text: Turn off screening during games and switch it back on for the off-season.
options.explanation: This removes the layer at the busiest and most visible time, which is the opposite of a safe default.

options.text: Let the main model screen its own input whenever the classifier times out.
options.explanation: Folding the screen into the main model removes the independent layer. The same model would judge input that may be trying to manipulate it.

stem: An internal HR assistant only answers benefits questions today, but it was given three tools: read_policy, update_salary and terminate_employee, the last two "for future features." To reduce risk, the team plans to add a classifier that detects misuse of the write tools. What is the better first step?

options.text: Add the classifier plus a system-prompt rule never to call the write tools.
options.explanation: Both measures try to stop misuse of capability the assistant doesn't need. A filter or rule can fail, and the tools would still be there.

options.text: Keep the tools but require Claude to explain its reasoning before each call.
options.explanation: An explanation from the model is not a control. Injected or mistaken reasoning can justify the call just as easily.

options.text: Keep the tools and log every call so misuse is caught after it happens.
options.explanation: Logging supports monitoring, but by the time someone reads the log a salary may already have changed or an employee been removed.

options.text: Remove the write tools until a feature needs them, leaving read_policy.
options.explanation: Correct. Least privilege means removing capability the use case doesn't need. That beats screening for misuse of tools that shouldn't exist.

stem: A team's merchandise chatbot handles order questions in which fans often type home addresses and partial card numbers. Engineers want to keep complete raw transcripts in the shared logging platform indefinitely to make debugging easier. Which approach follows secure-by-design privacy practice?

options.text: Keep full transcripts but restrict log access to the engineering team.
options.explanation: Access control helps, but the logs would still hold sensitive personal data forever, which widens the impact of any breach or insider misuse.

options.text: Redact personal data before logging and set a retention period on transcripts.
options.explanation: Correct. Privacy by design means collecting only what is needed, redacting before logging and limiting retention, while keeping enough data to debug.

options.text: Keep raw transcripts but ask Claude to leave personal data out of its replies.
options.explanation: The fans' own messages still contain the data. Instructing the model does nothing about what the logging pipeline stores.

options.text: Disable logging entirely so that no personal data is ever stored anywhere.
options.explanation: This removes the monitoring layer that guardrails depend on. Redaction and retention keep observability without hoarding personal data.

stem: A platform team runs Claude Code unattended on a shared build server in bypassPermissions mode so it never stops for approval. To keep it safe, they rely on a carefully written list of allow rules naming the only commands it should run. What is wrong with this design, and what is a better one?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because allow rules limit bypass mode to the listed commands.
options.explanation: Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions, so the list restricts nothing. Every other command runs without a prompt.

options.text: The list is fine, but it should move into CLAUDE.md so Claude reads it each run.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is guidance the model reads, not enforcement. It would make the list advisory rather than fix it.

options.text: Allow rules don't restrict that mode; use dontAsk with allow and deny rules in an isolated container.
options.explanation: Correct. In bypassPermissions, allow rules have no effect, though deny rules still apply. dontAsk denies anything not pre-approved, and isolation limits damage from what slips through.

options.text: Switch to auto mode instead, since its classifier approves exactly the commands that the allow list names.
options.explanation: Auto mode uses a classifier to review actions. It does not turn the allow list into an exclusive whitelist, so it does not enforce the intended boundary.

stem: A youth-focused fan app has a written content policy: answer questions about stats, schedules and rules, and refuse betting advice. The policy currently exists only in the system prompt. Which two additions best enforce the same policy at other layers? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Screen incoming messages against the policy with a fast classifier model.
options.explanation: Correct. An input screen checks the same policy before the request reaches the main model, which adds an independent layer.

options.text: Check each reply against the policy before it is shown to the user.
options.explanation: Correct. Output checks catch policy violations that got past the prompt and the input screen.

options.text: Restate the policy in a second, longer system prompt for emphasis.
options.explanation: This is still the model layer. More instructions do not add enforcement anywhere else.

options.text: Give Claude a betting-odds tool so it recognizes gambling questions.
options.explanation: Adding a capability the policy forbids widens what can go wrong, which is the opposite of least privilege.

options.text: Rely on Claude's built-in safety training to refuse betting questions.
options.explanation: General safety training doesn't encode this app's specific policy. Betting information isn't harmful in general, so the app must enforce its own rule.

stem: A league office's agent updates player contract records, and it currently runs under a shared administrator service account for every request. An audit flags this as a risk. Which two changes follow secure-by-design identity and access practice? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Give the agent its own workload identity with only the permissions it needs.
options.explanation: Correct. A dedicated identity with least privilege limits what a compromised or mistaken agent can do and makes its actions traceable.

options.text: Have the agent act with the requesting user's rights or narrower, checked in code.
options.explanation: Correct. The agent should never be able to do more than the user it acts for, and that check must be enforced in code rather than by the model.

options.text: Keep one administrator account across all agents to simplify the audit trail.
options.explanation: Sharing an administrator identity maximizes the blast radius and makes it harder to attribute actions to a specific agent.

options.text: Let Claude decide which permission level each incoming request deserves.
options.explanation: Authorization decisions made by the model can be manipulated. Access levels must be decided by application code.

options.text: Put the administrator password in the system prompt for occasional elevation.
options.explanation: Secrets in the prompt can leak through output, and elevation on the model's say-so defeats least privilege.

stem: A club's marketing agent can draft and send emails to all 60,000 season-ticket holders. A drafting mistake would reach every fan and can't be recalled. The team still wants the agent to do the drafting. Which guardrail best fits?

options.text: Require a human to approve each bulk send before the tool executes it
options.explanation: Correct. Irreversible, high-impact actions call for human approval. The agent keeps the drafting work, and a person confirms the one step that can't be undone.

options.text: Tell the agent in its system prompt to double-check every email carefully before sending it
options.explanation: A prompt instruction is advisory. It reduces mistakes but doesn't stop one from reaching every fan.

options.text: Log every email the agent sends so the team can review them each Monday morning
options.explanation: A weekly review finds the problem after 60,000 fans have already received the email.

options.text: Switch to a larger model, which makes fewer drafting mistakes on long emails
options.explanation: A stronger model lowers the error rate but still allows an unrecallable mistake through with no check.

stem: A scouting agent reads public web pages and runs Python on a club's private draft board. The security team worries that instructions hidden in a web page could make the agent send the draft board to an attacker's server. Input screening is already in place. Which additional layer best limits the damage if an injection gets through?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt forbidding the agent from uploading data anywhere
options.explanation: A successful injection is exactly the case where the model may not follow its instructions, so this layer fails in the same way as the one it backs up.

options.text: Run the agent in a sandboxed container whose network egress is limited to an allowlist of needed domains
options.explanation: Correct. An infrastructure control fails differently from prompt-level defences: even a fully hijacked agent can't reach a server outside the allowlist.

options.text: Use a second, more capable model to rephrase every web page before the agent reads it
options.explanation: Rephrasing may weaken some injections, but it is another model-level defence and doesn't stop data leaving the network.

options.text: Review the agent's logs at the end of each week for any unusual outbound requests
options.explanation: Monitoring helps detect incidents, but a weekly review comes long after the draft board has leaked.

stem: A SaaS vendor hosts one Claude-based assistant for 30 football clubs. Every club's private scouting reports sit in a shared vector store. A club must never see another club's reports, even if a user asks cleverly. Which design best enforces this?

options.text: Put each user's club name in the system prompt and instruct Claude to quote only that club's reports
options.explanation: Other clubs' reports would still be retrieved into context, and a prompt instruction can be talked around.

options.text: Run an output filter that removes any other club's name from responses before display
options.explanation: Filters miss paraphrases, and the data has already reached the model. Isolation should stop it being retrieved at all.

options.text: Ask users to confirm their club at the start of each chat and trust the answer for retrieval
options.explanation: A self-reported club is an unverified claim, so anyone can name a rival club.

options.text: Filter retrieval in code by the authenticated user's tenant, so other clubs' reports never reach the model
options.explanation: Correct. Tenant isolation enforced in the retrieval layer, from a verified identity, means the model never sees data it isn't allowed to reveal.

stem: A new agent feature that can change fans' account settings is launching. Operations wants to be able to stop it within minutes if it starts misbehaving, without affecting the rest of the app. Which control best fits?

options.text: Revoke the API key if something goes wrong.
options.explanation: Revoking the key stops every Claude feature in the app, not just this one, and someone then has to rotate it.

options.text: Add "Stop if you are misbehaving" to the system prompt.
options.explanation: A misbehaving agent can't be relied on to stop itself.

options.text: Roll back with a normal code deploy.
options.explanation: A deploy is usually slower than minutes and risks taking unrelated changes back with it.

options.text: A feature flag (kill switch) that disables the agent's write tools, or the whole feature, at runtime without a deploy, combined with a staged rollout and alerting.
options.explanation: Correct. A runtime switch gives fast, targeted containment. Staged rollout and alerting limit how many users are affected and how long it takes to notice.

stem: A free public trivia bot calls Claude from the company's backend. Last weekend a handful of scripted accounts generated most of the month's token spend. Which TWO guardrails best address this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Monitor usage per user and alert on anomalies, such as sudden spikes or request patterns that look automated.
options.explanation: Correct. Monitoring catches abuse that gets past static limits, and catches it quickly.

options.text: Rely on the organization's API rate limits to share capacity fairly between users.
options.explanation: Organization-level limits apply to the app as a whole and know nothing about individual end users.

options.text: Enforce per-user and per-session rate limits and token quotas in the application.
options.explanation: Correct. Limits per user in the app stop a few accounts from consuming shared capacity and budget.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so that each answer is complete and users send fewer follow-ups.
options.explanation: This doesn't limit abusive request volume and makes each request more expensive.

options.text: Move the API key into the front end in obfuscated form so that the backend isn't involved.
options.explanation: Shipping the key to clients exposes it to everyone and removes the server-side point of control.

stem: Three engineers built a club's fan chatbot separately: one wrote the system prompt, one tuned an input classifier, and one wrote an output filter. In testing, the classifier blocks injury-report questions that the prompt allows, and the filter lets betting tips through that the prompt forbids. What should the team do first?

options.text: Drop the classifier and the filter, and rely on the system prompt as the one source of intent.
options.explanation: This removes the layers that enforce anything. A prompt alone guides behavior but cannot guarantee it, so one clever message could defeat the whole design.

options.text: Write one content policy for topics, actions and refusals, and derive every layer from it.
options.explanation: Correct. Layers only add up when they enforce the same written policy. Defining it once and expressing it in the prompt, the classifier and the filter removes both the over-blocking and the gap.

options.text: Keep all three as they are, since layers that disagree are harder for attackers to predict.
options.explanation: Inconsistent layers are not defense in depth. They block legitimate fans in one place and leave forbidden content unchecked in another.

options.text: Make every layer refuse anything that any of the others would flag, so the strictest rule wins.
options.explanation: Merging inconsistent rules keeps the injury-question over-blocking and still leaves no layer that reliably catches betting tips. The missing piece is an agreed policy, not more strictness.

stem: A club is adding a feature in which Claude suggests merchandise based on a fan's purchase history. Each fan's CRM record also holds a home address, date of birth and payment details. Which THREE choices follow secure-by-design privacy practice? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Send Claude the full CRM record so it has every detail it might use to personalize suggestions.
options.explanation: This sends data the task does not need. Addresses, birth dates and payment details add leak risk without improving merchandise suggestions.

options.text: Send Claude only the purchase-history fields that the suggestion task actually needs.
options.explanation: Correct. Data minimization is the first privacy control: data that never reaches the model can never leak from it.

options.text: Tell Claude in the system prompt never to mention addresses or payment details in replies.
options.explanation: A prompt instruction is advisory and leaves the sensitive data in context. Not sending it is the stronger control.

options.text: Load only the signed-in fan's record, looked up in code from the authenticated session.
options.explanation: Correct. Scoping data to the authenticated user in code keeps other fans' records out of the context, whatever the conversation asks for.

options.text: Let Claude look up any fan's record by name, so it can compare buying patterns across fans.
options.explanation: This grants the model access to every customer's data. Any injection or confused request could then expose other fans' records.

options.text: Redact personal data from prompts and replies before logging them, and set a retention period.
options.explanation: Correct. Logs are a common leak path. Redacting before logging and limiting retention keeps observability without storing personal data indefinitely.
